newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Appetites whetted for East Europe forex.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Appetites whetted for East Europe forex.

text.p: The taste for currency trading in eastern Europe has been whetted by the turbulence in the Czech crown and Polish zloty in recent months and analysts believe the promise of further liberalisation, greater liquidity and new products sharpens the appetite.

The prospect of European Union membership, the likely disappearance of many western European currencies after European monetary union in 1999 and relatively rich pickings for yield-hungry investors make the region a sure bet long-term, London analysts said.
But markets are impatient and so-called "financial engineers" and "rocket-scientists" have already been at work to design ways to beat the rush.

"The movements in Czech and Polish currencies did inject some uncertainty into what had been predominantly (interest rate) carry trades," said Andrew Kenningham, east Europe fixed income economist at Merrill Lynch.

"What's happened with the Czech crown, for example, as it became more and more liquid and trading bands widened, is that it became much more of a (currency) trading market and less of a carry trade," said Kenningham.

The preponderance of carry trades -- buying high-yielding short-term securities such as Treasury bills purely for the interest rate return -- had been enhanced by the predictability of heavily controlled currency regimes.

With interest rates on one-year T-bills, for example, in excess of 20 percent and official currency policies based either on fixed pegs or managed depreciation, net returns are both potentially large and easily calculable.
But the crux for carry trades is that currency movements can be estimated in advance.
The play loses its lustre if there is a perceived risk that the currency could fall up to 30 percent over the period, or there are large and frequent swings as in Poland's case recently.

With the notable exception of the Czech market, currency trading by foreigners in countries such as Poland, Russia, Slovakia or Hungary is restricted. To be able to hedge, that is limit risk from entering these markets, or to speculate, investors resorted to derivative instruments.
NDF A FEATURE OF FOREIGN PARTICIPATION
Over the past year a market in contracts called non-deliverable forward (NDF) has been a central feature of rising foreign participation in the region.
The nub of this market is that it avoids the settlement procedure and paper work and the problems of getting in and out of highly illiquid currency forward markets.

In Poland, for example, you can only buy dollars forward if you can prove there is an import bill to pay. This exclusive matching of importers and exporters makes for a very illiquid market where the bid/offer spreads become prohibitive.

For NDF's, however, you can either hedge the currency risk on an underlying asset or you can take a position in the currency without the local unit ever changing hands. All you agree is a contract for differences in the price and settle in a benchmark currency like the dollar.

"Sales guys in these markets get up to all sorts of tricks to avoid exchange controls and central bank restrictions but NDF's have become the favourite conduit," said Miranda Xafa, senior analyst at Salomon Brothers.
The main NDF centres are London and New York and hedging is often arranged via securities transactions with local banks.

Analysts said the NDF's may be seen as dangerous by central banks because they escape control, but ultimately they are encouraging long-term. When the region's currencies become fully convertible much of the volume in NDF's will translate to greater daily turnover in local currency.

"Countries like Poland are reluctant to liberalise the (foreign exchange) market for now and they are probably correct. It is better to do it after you've achieved macro-economic stability and after the economy has been restructured," said Xafa. "Otherwise you are more fragile, more open to sudden changes in the investors sentiment."
CZECH REPUBLIC'S MARKET A BENCHMARK

The Czech Republic's wide open market has become the benchmark for future currency market liberalisation in the region and an illustration of how much currency markets can grow when the barriers are removed.

The crown's plunge in May following a deteriorating economic outlook showed the dangers of too great liberalisation which is not accompanied by sound economic policies and restructuring of the real economy.

Daily turnover in the crown prior to the trouble in May was in excess of $5 billion, compared to less than $500 million in zlotys at present. Turnover of Hungarian forints and Slovak crowns is less than $150-$200 million a day.

"The full convertibility of the Czech crown led to a massive amount of short-term foreign capital playing the market. But once there was a sense the economic balance was unsustainable then that short-term money just said goodbye," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
Because of the lack of exchange controls, a substantial offshore market in crowns, or eurocrowns, developed. It was centred in London and, to a lesser extent, in New York.

This offshore market was fuelled by a wave of Czech crown eurobonds issued last year and early this. More than a billion dollars of crown eurobonds were sold in 1996 and almost two billion dollars' worth were issued in early 1997 alone.

When crown selling went from a trickle to a flood in May, central bank intervention on the local market proved fruitless as speculators and hedgers had access to crown liquidity outside Prague. As a result, it was possible to borrow crowns for short selling in London and even informal controls on lending crowns to overseas players had only a limited effect.
LONG-TERM LIBERALISATION IS CERTAIN

Analysts agreed that convertibility is just a matter of time and that the zloty, forint and other currencies from the region will sooner or later become as accessible as Italian lire, Swedish crowns and Spanish pesetas.

"Ironically, these countries probably aspire to monetary union down the road but to get there they have to free up their currencies first and go through the same experience France, Italy and Sweden have gone through over the past 15 years," said one analyst at a Swiss Bank here.
The Czech example shows that a country's exposure to foreign capital may increase even earlier once hedge funds, highly leveraged, speculative investors, begin to prowl for yields.

Data collected by TASS Management Ltd shows hedge fund returns in emerging market debt as a whole at 35.5 percent in the 12 months to March 1997 and their returns in emerging market equity was a whopping 68.8 percent over the same period.
"A lot of new people began getting into these markets and a lot of the (yield) spreads got tighter and tighter -- to levels you would never have believed," said Kenningham at Merrill.
And it is the hedge funds who pioneer and take advantage of the derivative instruments such as NDFs and other less popular ones being developed on the market.
